The men who defend the King James to the last page are defending an Old Testament settled by the rabbis who rejected Christ. The apostles read another one. You can see the seam in your own Bible in under a minute, with no original languages at all. Take a King James, find a place where an apostle quotes the Old Testament, and turn to the verse he is quoting. The two do not always match. Begin with the epistle to the Hebrews.

That letter puts these words in the mouth of Christ as He enters the world:

“Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me.” - Hebrews 10:5, KJV

He is quoting a psalm. Turn to it in the same King James and the sentence is gone. There Psalm 40:6 reads:

“Mine ears hast thou opened...” - Psalm 40:6, KJV

Ears. Not a body. The Greek psalm the apostle held in his hands says what he says:

“Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not; but a body hast thou prepared me.” - Psalm 39:7, LXX

Same verse, two different sentences, one binding. That is one seam. There are more.

Two More Seams

Luke records Jesus standing in the synagogue at Nazareth, reading from Isaiah:

“...he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind...” - Luke 4:18, KJV

Now open Isaiah 61:1 in the same King James:

“...he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound...” - Isaiah 61:1, KJV

The sight to the blind is gone. The Septuagint has it:

“...to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind.” - Isaiah 61:1, LXX

The sentence Jesus read as his own mission is missing from the Old Testament printed in the same binding.

Stephen, on trial before the council, quotes Amos and names a false god:

“...the star of your god Remphan...” - Acts 7:43, KJV

Turn to Amos 5:26 in the same King James and the god has another name:

“...the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god...” - Amos 5:26, KJV

Stephen's name is the Septuagint's:

“...the star of your god Ræphan...” - Amos 5:26, LXX

Stephen was reading Greek.

Hebrews, Luke, Acts. In each one the apostles stand on the Greek, and the Old Testament in your binding stands on the Hebrew. The King James, the ESV, the NASB, and the NIV all rest on a Hebrew text settled by the rabbis who rejected Christ. How did that happen, and what does it cost you?

A Fight Older Than the Reformation

The church knew about the seam. For its first centuries it read the Greek Old Testament. Around AD 400, Jerome went back to the Hebrew for his Latin translation and called it the Hebrew truth. Augustine objected, because the churches had read the Greek for generations and he did not want a rope pulled out from under them. Jerome's way eventually carried the West.

A thousand years later the Reformers, hungry for the original languages and eager to cut loose from Rome, went to the Hebrew too. The King James translators built their Old Testament mainly on a Hebrew edition printed in Venice in 1524, known as the Second Rabbinic Bible. Read that title again. Rabbinic Bible.

The Eastern churches never made the turn. The Orthodox kept the Greek Old Testament, and the Ethiopian church carried it into Ge'ez, where it still stands inside an eighty-one book canon.

The instinct to go back to the Hebrew was not foolish. Wanting the original language is an honorable hunger. The trouble sits in the question that follows: which Hebrew, and who settled it?

Who Held the Pen

The Dead Sea Scrolls show Hebrew Scripture running in more than one stream before Christ. Some scrolls look like the later Masoretic text. Others stand with the Septuagint. After the Temple fell in AD 70, the rabbinic movement, the heirs of the men who rejected Jesus as Messiah, gathered around one stream, and the others stopped being copied in Judaism. Centuries later the Masoretes, working between the sixth and tenth centuries, fixed that stream's vowels and its final form. The oldest complete copies of their text, the Aleppo and Leningrad codices, come from the tenth and eleventh centuries.

The Hebrew under your Old Testament did not come to you from the apostles' church. It came through a tradition that had already answered the question of Christ with a no, and that tradition held the pen whenever two readings met. Where the stream they chose and the stream the apostles quoted come apart, the apostles' stream lost its seat. That is why these three verses split the way they do.

The Irony at the KJV Table

This is the part KJV defenders should sit with. Their case against the modern New Testament runs on age and pedigree: the older line, the purer line, and a deep suspicion of Alexandria. Hold their own Old Testament to that standard. The Hebrew under the King James has complete copies a thousand years after Christ, was settled by the tradition that rejected him, and reached the translators in a volume called the Rabbinic Bible. The Greek the apostles quoted was translated in Alexandria itself, centuries before Christ, and in places the Dead Sea Scrolls stand with it against the later Hebrew. Complete Greek Old Testaments from the fourth century are older than any complete Hebrew codex we have.

A man cannot demand the oldest witness for the New Testament and wave it off for the Old because the church grew used to the other.

I took the KJV-only argument apart on its own terms in The KJV-Only Myth and traced the translators' own admissions in The King's English. This is the same standard applied one testament earlier. The longer evidence, including the pierced hands of the Psalm and the sons of God in Moses' song, is in The Bible in Your Hand Is Not the Bible Jesus Read.

Read Both, Then Let the Apostles Judge

Where the two texts agree, and they agree in most places, you lose nothing. Where they split and the apostles stand on the Greek, give that reading the weight the New Testament itself gives it. Keep your Bible. Know what it stands on. The apostles built on the Greek Old Testament. A Bible that sets the rabbis' Hebrew above it has moved the foundation stone, and every church that copied the move inherited it without being told.

Know the stone you are standing on. Then go back and read the one the apostles stood on.

If you own a King James, put Psalm 40:6 and Hebrews 10:5 side by side tonight and tell me what you see.
